_: Hand-written prose for the roadmap's request-driven entries. NOT a list of what is
on the page — the issue tracker is that, and this file cannot add or remove an entry.
WHAT DECIDES WHETHER SOMETHING APPEARS, and where:
enhancement + accepted    -> 'From your requests'. I am going to build this.
enhancement + considered  -> 'Later / maybe'. Interesting, not committed.
bug + accepted            -> 'Known bugs' (see bugs.json).
no `accepted` / `considered`  -> nowhere. Filing publishes nothing.
closed                    -> nowhere, immediately. Shipping or refusing a thing and
closing its issue is the only bookkeeping there is.
Labels, in other words — not this file. Applying one needs Triage, so the gate is
closed to the people who file and open to me, which is the point: the roadmap is a
published page and everything on it is something I am asserting.
Promotion is a label edit: `considered` -> `accepted` moves an entry from Later /
maybe into its own card, and nothing here changes.
manual — YOURS, and the only way onto this page for something nobody filed. One
entry per file in docs/plans/: a planning agent designs a feature, its
plan lands there, and this is how the roadmap says it is coming without
waiting for a ticket somebody opens about their own project. Same shape
and same reasoning as bugs.json's manual[], which has always had it.
title      the heading
railLabel  shorter label for the contents rail (optional)
html       the body, as lines of HTML
id         anchor (optional; derived from the title otherwise)
plan       the docs/plans/ filename this speaks for. NOT rendered — it
is what lets the periodic sweep tell an entry whose plan has
shipped from one whose plan is still open, without matching
on prose.
issue      optional. Where one exists this entry replaces what the
reporter wrote, and closing the issue still retires it.
shipped_in optional. Set it and the entry stops rendering — the same
bookkeeping every other kind of entry has.
overrides — keyed by issue number as a string. A generated entry is a starting
point, not a verdict: whatever is here wins over what the reporter
wrote. The issue decides THAT it appears; this decides how it reads.
title      replace the heading
railLabel  shorter label for the contents rail
html       replace the body outright, as lines of HTML. Once set, the
reporter's prose is no longer rendered — carry over
anything that mattered.
note       append one paragraph, keeping the reporter's prose
near       the § section it sits beside
A § number is a POSITION in the backlog and moves whenever I reorder it, so any
§n written here — in `near`, or in `html` prose — is a thing that can go stale in
a commit that never touched this file. Always pair one with its anchor
(`§5`); the anchor is a content slug and does not move,
and `roadmap-data.mjs --check` will not catch a number that is merely wrong.
credit     GitHub handle to thank. Asked-for, not written-by.
hide       true to keep the label and stay off the page
Refusing something is not recorded here and never appears: close it, and if the
reason is a boundary worth writing down it earns a card in 'Considered and set
aside' in roadmap.html by hand. A no should cost me a sentence.
Render with `node scripts/roadmap-data.mjs`.

manual.title: Reading comfort and a contrast switch
html: A contrast switch in Settings, and the palette work it needs: ink and hairline
contrast raised to WCAG AA in all four aesthetics, resolving to the same state
as the prefers-contrast: more media query rather than fighting it.
Alongside it, the reading-comfort controls the quote text itself has never had —
size, line height and measure — on top of the serif/sans choice
Settings → Type already offers. A dyslexia-friendly face, already reachable by
upload and never offered, gets bundled and named. And every gesture this app
ships gains a named, focusable equivalent, so a drag or a swipe is never the
only way to reach a thing.

manual.title: Anthologies that fill themselves, and export as a book
html: A rule — the same facets the search bar already speaks — fills an anthology
with matching quotes in one press. It only ever appends: a fill never removes
and never reorders, so your order and your commentary are never disturbed by
running it again, and it reports what it could not fit rather than dropping
quotes quietly.
Then a real shelf to put the result on: EPUB, a zip the
standard library already knows how to write, so the collection reads on the
same reader the highlights came off, and a proper print stylesheet for Print →
Save as PDF. Both read the same field registry the reading view does, widened
to reach the work's own record and an author's or character's own portrait and
dates — so an anthology can look like a small book instead of a list.

manual.title: Atrium, the glass material set
html: atrium is the eighth material set and the only one still a
placeholder — four flat tiles reserving a slot for something translucent and
lit from behind, built to Apple's own Liquid Glass guidance: a functional layer
for the rail, the top bar and sheets, never the cards a board scrolls past, with
a real edge that bends light rather than a faked rim.
Getting there starts by fixing a live defect the design pass found: choosing
Atrium today saves nothing, because the server does not yet know the name. From
there, the glass itself — a blur that actually turns off under reduced
transparency, an accent that stays a light rather than a colour, and a
performance budget measured on a real board before a line of CSS ships, not
assumed after.

manual.title: One field table for both bulk editors
html: The staged bulk editor and the live one read from two hand-written field lists
that have quietly drifted apart, and neither list is a superset of the other —
a season set before approval cannot be changed after, and a note added after
approval could never have been set before. One shared field table, in Go,
replaces both: every bulk-settable column named once, with the kinds it applies
to, its validation, and whether clearing it writes an empty value or leaves it
alone.
Each screen keeps the control its job needs — the queue sets many fields at
once across a mixed batch, the library sets one carefully with the right
editor for it and a warning saying what it will overwrite. What they stop
keeping is a private list: a test walks each panel against the table, in both
directions, so a field one screen gains and the other loses fails the build
instead of drifting for a release.

manual.title: The library remembers what you already typed
html: Every locator in this app is free text, and free text typed twice is typed
differently — "The Fall" beside "the fall", chapter 3 beside chapter 03. This
offers back your own prior values as you type — on the add form, the edit form,
import review and bulk edit — and where two fields are paired, picking one can
fill the other.
Filling is careful rather than eager: a blank field fills silently, a field
that already disagrees is offered as a chip and never overwritten without a
tap. Every offer chip carries its own Alt+1–9, so the keyboard
route never collides with the numeric field the chip sits beside.
Season-and-episode pairing waits on
episode names existing to pair with.

manual.title: Episode names, and up to three orderings
html: A series episode has never had anywhere to hold a name — only
the season and episode numbers it airs under. This gives it one, plus up to
three orders to view it by: broadcast, a published DVD or streaming order, and
a hand-built custom one — because some shows, Firefly among them, were
never watched in the order they aired.
Names and the alternate order can be fetched from the same providers the
library already trusts, never automatically and never overwriting a name typed
by hand. Reordering gets a real drag control, built once and shared with the
anthology entry list, with a keyboard route from the outset rather than added
later. It splits off the entry-form work that
discovered the gap, and either can ship first.

manual.title: Import: one drop target, however the file is typed
html: Replaces the wall of seven format cards with one row that is also a drop
target: drop a file, or choose one, and the server reads the bytes to work out
what it is — never the extension, never what the file picker was told to
expect. The list of what is supported moves into help, where a list belongs,
and a file dropped in the wrong place is named for what it actually is — a
backup archive, an EPUB, an image — rather than met with a bare "unrecognised".
Along the way, a Readest JSON export becomes a source of its
own — it carries the highlight colour and the reading progress the Markdown
export loses — and the Markdown parser gets back the notes and timestamps it
currently drops on the floor.

manual.title: Locators from files — dialogue timestamps and ebook locations
html: Drop a subtitle file (SRT, VTT, ASS/SSA) or an ebook
(EPUB, MOBI/AZW3) beside a dialogue or book, and the app reads
it to find where each quote appears — as a timestamp for dialogue, as a location
or chapter for ebooks. The positions are proposed for review in a new Checks
section before applying, never stored in the file itself, and matched through
the same deduplication fold the library already uses, so an apostrophe means the
same thing in both.
An ambiguous match carries both candidates and the evidence — the matched text —
so the eye can decide. A file for the wrong cut says so instead of writing 200
wrong times. A refusal is durable: reject one proposal and it stays rejected on
the next scan, the same model Cleanup uses. Dropping one file on one work opens
a screen listing every cue or paragraph with your own matches already
highlighted, so a fuzzy one is checked by eye rather than accepted blind.

manual.title: Source files — a work keeps the file its quotes came from
html: A quote out of context can read as nonsense, and until now a work has never
kept the file its quotes came from. This gives it one source file per role — a
subtitle track for a film, an ebook for a book — arriving either uploaded or
found on a read-only mount of your own library, the route that scales past
uploading one file at a time.
What the file is for is stored the moment it is read: where each quote sits,
and the text around it, so a position and a
quote's context both survive the file being deleted. Once every quote from a
work has that context saved, the raw file itself can be thrown away — measured
at 29 times smaller than keeping it — and added again later if new quotes need
placing. Nothing here is a reader: no rendering, no pagination, no download, and
nothing fetched from anywhere.

manual.title: Spaced repetition — three difficulties and a longer ceiling
html: The 100-day ceiling goes to 365 — the longest interval the
research actually measured — which raises the library size the review loop can
keep current from about 800 quotes to about 2,900. Alongside it, three
difficulty tiers plus Random change which directions are
asked, how distractors are chosen and how wide the cloze blank is: Easy trades
away the better-teaching close alternatives on purpose, to buy a lower floor;
Hard gives up recognition entirely and asks you to type the words back.
Underneath both, the adaptive scheduler becomes the default (the fixed ladder
stays as the opt-in), fed by a new append-only review log — the first record
of what was actually answered. That makes a true retention
figure possible, read against a target the reader sets rather than a hidden
50%, and a title earned from how many quotes have reached the long rungs
rather than from the retention number itself.

7.title: Richer author portraits
html: Resolve the author's Wikidata entry via the book, so a photo appears even
when the Open Library record is sparse. The disambiguation already picks the right
person; this only widens coverage, which is why it is small enough to say yes to.
It should land after §9, not before: once sources
are mine to pick, looking a person up should query Wikidata and not waste a call on
TMDB. Doing it in the other order would bake in the fan-out that section exists to end.

12.title: Audio review, in the browser only
html: Reading a due card aloud, using the browser's own SpeechSynthesis. It
costs the server nothing, needs no key, and works offline once <a
href="#mobile-pwa">§5's service worker
exists — which is the entire reason this can be accepted while server-side speech
stays refused. Those are not the same feature wearing different clothes: one is a
model and an audio pipeline on a box that cannot spare either, and the other is an
API the browser already ships.
Accepted rather than parked because the line it sat next to turned out to be drawn
in the right place already — see
OCR, and speech, on the server. Scope: a play control on a
review card and nothing else. No stored audio, no transcription, no server route.

2.title: AI summaries (opt-in)
html: A passive digest: batch recent highlights and summarise them with an
OpenAI-compatible model — local or remote, your endpoint, your key.
Grouped by book, tag or whole library; weekly or on-demand. Off unless configured,
generated async, and — true to the frugality goal — no cron dependency.
The digest has to be worth opening in the app on its own before any question of pushing
it arises, which is why delivery is the separate entry below and neither one waits on
the other.

3.title: Notifications (opt-in)
html: Would start with NTFY, likely routed through a multi-service notifier such as <a
href="https://containrrr.dev/shoutrrr/">Shoutrrr so one config reaches any backend —
the email digest fallback below is that same slot with a different
transport. Non-negotiable, whatever I pick: <strong>high / urgent priority must carry
through — a resurfaced highlight is a gentle nudge, but "lookup is failing"
should be able to shout, and that case alone justifies this even if no summary ever gets

generated.
This sat in the numbered backlog until I moved it here deliberately,
because anything that pushes needs something that wakes up on its own. The cheap end of
the ask needs none of it: the app-icon badge already shipped and shows a due-card
count with no server work and nothing scheduled.

4.title: Anki export / import
html: — bridge the daily review to and from Anki decks (.apkg), a natural pairing
for the spaced-repetition audience. Still being scoped; I need to learn the format
first.

5.title: Backlinks & freeform notes
html: — manually-maintained links between related highlights, Zettelkasten-style, and
standalone notes not tied to any book. Kept deliberately manual; no auto-suggested
"related" magic.

6.title: Shared / household libraries
html: — collaborative or shared-view libraries across the users on one box.

8.title: Email digest fallback
html: (SMTP) — the same delivery slot as the notifier above, for people who would rather not
run one.

9.title: Semantic search
html: (sqlite-vec) — a dependency, an indexing pass and a model, on a box budgeted
at 20–40 MB RSS. Deferred indefinitely rather than left unsaid: the two read the same
from outside and only one of them is honest.

10.title: Summary export
html: to Markdown / Obsidian.

11.title: Reviving a rating
html: The 1–5 stars were retired on purpose in 0.4.3 and ♥ is the cleaner
signal, so this is recorded as a reversal to weigh rather than as planned work — but
half-stars are the single most-cited feature of the trackers people arrive from, and the
columns are still there, inert, from before the drop. If it ever comes back it should be
per-user and opt-in, so the default library looks exactly as it does now.

13.title: A voice note on a quote
html: — record, store, play back, with no transcription, which would be a dependency. For the
reaction you can't type while reading.
